item.title: US to make visa bond programme permanent for people from dozens of countries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B

The US State Department will make permanent a visa bond programme that could require applicants from 50 countries, mostly from Africa, to post bonds of up to $20,000 when seeking US visas, according to a federal notice posted online on Friday.

The Federal Register notice applies to B1 and B2 visas, which are issued for business and tourism travel.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

“The 2025 visa bond pilot, which provided a framework for the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of the Treasury to assess the feasibility of administering a visa bond programme, has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond programme is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In the pilot programme, consular officers could require bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or up to $15,000. The final rule eliminates the $5,000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The final rule goes into effect on August 3 when it is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register. In the list of 50 countries for whose citizens this programme applies, 30 are from Africa.

US officials say the policy is intended to reduce visa overstays. Immigration advocates argue it will deter legitimate travel to the United States.

Rights advocates say President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown violates free speech and due process, while creating an unsafe environment for ethnic minorities and encouraging racial profiling. Trump has defended the measures as necessary to bolster national security.

While Trump says he wants to curb illegal immigration, his administration has made legal immigration more difficult, for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country.

Earlier in May, the State Department identified nationals from the following 50 countries as being required to post visa bonds: Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Benin, Bhutan, Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Central African Republic, Cote D’Ivoire, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ethiopia, Fiji, Gabon, The Gambia, Georgia, Grenada, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kyrgyz Republic, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

The revelation that 54 prisons across Bangladesh lack ambulances is nothing short of shocking. At a time when our country should be trying to modernize its justice and correctional systems, the fact that thousands of inmates have no access to emergency transport exposes a severe and dangerous gap in basic state responsibility and an utter disregard for humanity. Prisons house some of the most vulnerable people - individuals with limited access to healthcare, often living in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions, and frequently suffering from chronic illnesses. When medical emergencies occur, delays can and have been fatal with the lack of timely care. This is unacceptable, and calls for a very basic understanding that inmates in prison are human beings as well and deserve to be treated as such. We have, at this point, a correctional system that violates among the most fundamental principles of human rights -- the right to life and medical treatment. The state simply cannot ignore this issue any longer. Allocating ambulances to every prison should not be seen as a luxury but rather a minimum requirement. However, the solution must go beyond vehicles. Bangladesh needs a comprehensive overhaul of prison healthcare, including trained medical staff, functioning clinics, emergency equipment, and clear protocols for rapid response. Prisoners may be serving sentences, but they remain under the care of the state. Their health and safety should be non‑negotiable. A correctional system that cannot care for those within it is not one that can be looked at in a positive light. This is a state of affairs that demands immediate correction. Every prison should have the bare minimum capacity to protect the lives of those in its custody.

item.title: Creating a reliable railway system. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:

The announcement of more trains on the Dhaka-Cox’s Bazar route to address demand is undeniably positive. Rail connectivity to Cox’s Bazar has already transformed travel for millions, and adding another pair of trains will ease pressure on existing services, improve accessibility, and strengthen economic links between the capital and our most significant tourism hub. With that said, this development should be seen as part of a much larger national need: We have long needed to invest far more - and far more consistently - in our rail network. For decades, rail has been treated as a secondary mode of transport, overshadowed by highways and short‑term road expansion. The result is visible everywhere: Congested highways, unsafe long‑distance bus travel, rising transport emissions, and logistics bottlenecks that have slowed down our economy. Rail, by contrast, is safer, cleaner, more affordable, and far more efficient for both passengers and freight. The new Dhaka-Cox’s Bazar train pair is a step in the right direction, but we must see far more. We need a rail‑first development strategy that expands the capacity of our railways. As such, we expect the same urgency across all rail routes to all divisions. Freight corridors too must be strengthened so industries can move goods without relying solely on trucks. And regional links - including potential future connections with India, Nepal, and Bhutan - should be part of long‑term planning. Our ever-growing population and rising urbanization demand a transport system that can move people and goods reliably. Bangladesh has already invested heavily in megaprojects, sometimes unwisely. Now it must invest in the everyday infrastructure that keeps a country moving. The real goal should be clear: A modern, extensive, and reliable rail network that serves the entire nation.

The High Court’s order for the disposal of all pending applications for new passports and passport renewals filed by Bangladeshi expatriates within 60 days is certainly a welcome intervention but also exposes a much larger, persistent problem. Whether it is passports, land records, utility services, welfare benefits, or any other basic documentation, our public service delivery, despite lofty exclamations of digitization and reform, remains slow, fragmented, and deeply frustrating for ordinary citizens. The expat passport backlog is only one symptom of a system that struggles to keep pace with the country’s growing population, rising mobility, and expanding digital expectations. When expatriates, who contribute billions in remittances, face delays of weeks or months for something as fundamental as a passport, we must call it what it is: A structural failure. The same inefficiencies affect millions at home: Long queues, opaque procedures, inconsistent timelines, and a lack of accountability. The High Court’s directive is therefore less a procedural order and more a reminder that public service delivery must be fast, predictable, and citizen‑centred. We are a nation that aspires to reach middle‑income efficiency but that is impossible with our present outdated administrative practices. The solution requires systemic reform, and it begins with those in charge actually caring about doing their jobs properly. Better coordination rather than operating in silos and digital systems that are fully integrated, not partially adopted, should be the minimum expectation. Citizens deserve to receive timely responses instead of bureaucratic runarounds. Public services are not favours but rights. A modern Bangladesh demands modern service delivery, one that is transparent, efficient, and accountable, serving the best interest of the people.

item.title: The July Revolution and the reinvention of national purpose. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-20

Every generation inherits a defining historical moment. Some inherit liberation wars. Others inherit economic transformations or constitutional crises. The generation of Bangladesh that came of age in 2024 inherited something different: A civic uprising that fundamentally challenged the relationship between the citizen and the state. Two years after the July Revolution, political debates continue over who deserves credit, who bears responsibility, and whose narrative should ultimately dominate history. Governments have changed. Political alignments have shifted. New actors have emerged while old ones have disappeared from power. Yet if the anniversary of the July uprising teaches Bangladesh anything, it should be this: The true significance of those days extends far beyond partisan politics. The revolution ultimately became a test of whether Bangladesh could place the interests of the republic above the interests of competing political forces. That is why "Bangladesh First" carries far greater significance than a patriotic slogan. It offers an opportunity to revisit July not simply as a political movement but as a national moment of introspection. The essential question is no longer who won or who lost. Rather, it is whether Bangladesh itself became stronger through the crisis, and whether the painful lessons of those weeks are being translated into stronger institutions, greater accountability, and a more mature democratic culture. History repeatedly demonstrates that nations are transformed not merely by revolutions but by the lessons they choose to remember afterwards. France remembers 1789 differently from 1793. The United States remembers the Civil Rights Movement not only through legislation but through its continuing struggle with equality. South Africa continues to reinterpret the end of apartheid through debates about justice, reconciliation, and institutional reform. Likewise, Bangladesh's July Revolution should not become frozen as a monument belonging to one political generation. It should remain an evolving national conversation about citizenship, state power, public accountability and democratic responsibility. The greatest danger for any nation after a transformative political event is the temptation to reduce history to heroes and villains alone. Such narratives are emotionally satisfying but intellectually incomplete. They rarely explain why events unfolded as they did or why ordinary citizens suddenly became willing to assume extraordinary risks. Bangladesh deserves a more mature conversation. The July Revolution did not emerge suddenly on August 5. Nor was it born exclusively from the quota issue. Rather, the quota movement became the catalyst through which years of accumulated public frustration found organized expression. Understanding that distinction is essential for understanding modern Bangladesh. The quota issue was never only about quotas When the High Court restored the freedom fighter quota on June 5, 2024, many observers initially treated it as another legal controversy in Bangladesh's long history of disputes over public recruitment. Viewed in isolation, the judgment concerned administrative policy. Viewed within the broader socio-economic context, however, it touched one of the deepest anxieties facing contemporary Bangladesh. The country's demographic reality had changed dramatically over the previous decade. Bangladesh successfully expanded access to higher education, producing hundreds of thousands of university graduates every year. Yet economic expansion did not generate public-sector employment opportunities at a comparable pace. For many young graduates, government employment represented not merely a career but economic security, social mobility, and dignity. Consequently, recruitment policies became deeply symbolic. They represented competing visions of fairness itself. Supporters of quotas argued that the Liberation War deserved institutional recognition and that the sacrifices of freedom fighters should continue receiving state acknowledgement. Their argument rested upon historical justice. Opponents did not necessarily reject that history. Rather, they questioned whether historical recognition should continue shaping recruitment in ways they believed constrained meritocracy in a rapidly changing society. Their concern centred upon contemporary fairness. Both positions possessed moral foundations. The problem emerged because the national conversation increasingly ceased to distinguish disagreement from hostility. Instead of facilitating constructive debate regarding balancing historical obligations with present realities, political discourse gradually became polarized between competing moral absolutes. Once that occurred, compromise became increasingly difficult. The events that followed therefore cannot be understood merely as reactions to one judicial verdict. They reflected a deeper institutional challenge confronting Bangladesh: How should a nation honour its history without allowing historical memory itself to become a source of contemporary division? That question remains relevant today. From administrative dispute to national conversation The earliest demonstrations following the June 5 verdict remained remarkably restrained. Students organized peaceful processions, submitted memoranda, and appealed to constitutional institutions. Even during the first weeks, their strategy demonstrated an important characteristic that is often overlooked in retrospective political narratives. The movement initially expressed confidence in the state rather than rejection of it. This distinction deserves emphasis. Citizens protest because they expect governments to listen. Only when they gradually lose confidence in institutional responsiveness do demonstrations begin acquiring broader political significance. The students' memorandum to the Attorney General, their repeated appeals before the scheduled Supreme Court hearing, and their insistence upon legal remedies all suggested that the movement still believed constitutional mechanisms could resolve the dispute. In many respects, this reflected democratic maturity rather than political confrontation. History often forgets this early phase because later violence overshadows earlier restraint. Yet remembering it matters because it reveals that Bangladesh's institutions initially possessed opportunities for de-escalation. Whether those opportunities were fully utilized remains a question historians will continue debating. Why the movement spread beyond Dhaka By the beginning of July, something fundamentally changed. The demonstrations no longer remained confined to Dhaka University. Students from public universities across Bangladesh joined under the banner of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement. Within days, private universities also became increasingly engaged. Geographical expansion alone does not create a national movement. Shared emotional experience does. The speed with which the protests spread suggested that the quota issue had become a vessel carrying broader public frustrations. Across campuses, students increasingly interpreted the controversy as representing wider concerns regarding equality of opportunity, institutional responsiveness, youth unemployment and perceptions of exclusion. This phenomenon deserves careful analysis. Throughout modern history, transformative political movements rarely remain confined to their original grievances. The American Civil Rights Movement expanded beyond segregated buses. Poland's Solidarity movement grew beyond labour rights. The Arab Spring quickly moved beyond isolated acts of protest. Not because the original issues disappeared. Rather, because they revealed deeper structural frustrations already existing beneath the surface. Bangladesh followed a remarkably similar trajectory. The quota issue became the spark. The combustible material already existed. Perhaps no development illustrated this transformation more clearly than the emergence of the “Bangla blockade.” At first glance, blocking highways appears merely as another protest tactic. In reality, it represented an important shift in political strategy. Modern democracies are organized around shared public spaces. Roads, railway stations, bridges and major intersections connect citizens regardless of political affiliation or social class. Once those spaces become sites of political expression, the movement inevitably enters everyday national life. Until then, many Bangladeshis could observe events from a distance. The blockade made neutrality increasingly difficult. Office workers encountered demonstrations on their commute. Business owners experienced economic disruption. Parents worried about children travelling across cities. Citizens previously disengaged from politics suddenly found themselves participating emotionally because politics had entered their daily routines. Critics understandably questioned whether disrupting public life could ever be justified. Supporters argued that extraordinary institutional inaction required extraordinary civic pressure. Both arguments remain worthy of debate. However, irrespective of one's political position, the blockade undeniably succeeded in transforming a student protest into a national conversation. That strategic transformation proved historically decisive. The crisis of institutional communication One of the most revealing aspects of the early weeks was not the demonstrations themselves but the widening gap between institutional language and public perception. The government largely approached the situation through administrative and legal frameworks. Officials repeatedly emphasized that the matter remained before the courts and therefore required judicial resolution. Constitutionally, such reasoning appeared sound. Politically, however, it increasingly failed to resonate with protesters. This disconnect reflected a broader challenge confronting modern governance. Institutions often respond to procedural questions while citizens increasingly raise emotional ones. Governments speak about jurisdiction. Citizens speak about justice. Governments discuss legal timelines. Citizens measure political responsiveness. Neither conversation is necessarily incorrect. The problem emerges when neither side recognizes the legitimacy of the other's concerns. Bangladesh experienced precisely that communication breakdown. Each successive day widened the psychological distance between state institutions and student expectations. Once such gaps become sufficiently large, even well-intentioned policy responses struggle to restore confidence. Trust, after all, is far easier to lose than to rebuild. The politics of language Every political movement eventually encounters a symbolic moment that transforms its emotional character. For Bangladesh, that moment arrived on July 14. Until then, the movement had largely centred upon policy. Following the prime minister's remarks concerning " razakars ," the national conversation changed almost overnight. Political language matters because words do more than communicate.They define identity. The slogan that subsequently echoed across university campuses was not significant merely because it spread rapidly. Its deeper significance lay in how protesters transformed an accusation into satire. Throughout history, satire has often become one of the most powerful instruments of political resistance because it deprives authority of its monopoly over language. The July slogan demonstrated precisely that phenomenon. Whether one approved of the slogan or not, its impact upon public consciousness became undeniable. The movement was no longer debating administrative policy. It had entered the far more emotionally charged territory of dignity, recognition, and national identity. Once political conflicts become struggles over dignity rather than policy, compromise becomes significantly more difficult. Bangladesh was approaching that threshold. The first 40 days of the July Revolution therefore reveal a truth that should remain central to any honest historical assessment. Contrary to many later political interpretations, the movement did not begin as a campaign to overthrow a government. It began as an appeal for institutional responsiveness within the constitutional framework. Only gradually, through successive failures of communication, growing polarization, expanding public participation, and escalating confrontation, did it evolve into something much larger. Understanding that evolution matters because it contains perhaps the most important lesson for contemporary Bangladesh. Nations are rarely destabilized by one controversial decision alone. They are destabilized when institutions fail to recognize how individual decisions accumulate into broader crises of public confidence. For every future government -- regardless of ideology -- that may be the most enduring lesson of June and early July 2024. The republic is always strongest when citizens believe they can be heard before they feel compelled to be remembered. HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s words on the need for adopting innovative and environmentally-sustainable solutions to tackle riverbank erosion is timely and necessary, and must be heeded. Despite being among the most persistent and devastating challenges, we remain far from addressing them. In the meantime, every year, erosion destroys homes, cropland, roads, schools, and entire villages as families are displaced overnight, livelihoods vanish, and local economies collapse. While we continue to squander public funds, the PM’s directive should be clear: Solutions must be environmentally sound, scientifically grounded, and implemented through coordinated action, and crucially, must be completed within time and within budget - a standard that too many of our public projects fail to meet consistently. River erosion has long been treated with short‑term fixes which may slow damage temporarily, but do not address the underlying causes. Any meaningful solution must respect the rivers themselves. Restoring natural riverbanks, reinforcing them with vegetation, redesigning embankments to work with water flow rather than against it, and protecting wetlands that act as natural buffers are approaches that have been proven globally, and Bangladesh must now do all it can to implement them. The PM’s emphasis on coordination is also critical. River management cannot be handled by isolated agencies working independently, and working in silos has also consistently been among the failures of our governance. Equally important is financial discipline. Too many of our projects drag on for years, balloon in cost, or remain half‑finished while communities continue to suffer. We need projects that deliver measurable results and not symbolic gestures. The future will not get any easier for us, and we must move beyond reactive measures and commit to long‑term, science‑driven solutions that protect both our rivers and the millions who depend on them.

Even when fatal accidents occur, investigations are slow and consequences rare, reinforcing a culture of impunity that has become synonymous with our nation. As long as these issues are not addressed, we will not see any improvement in our quest for safer roads. The economic cost of road accidents is enormous while the human cost is immeasurable. item.title: Bangladesh hasn't given its students a bargain worth working hard for. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

Some years ago, I travelled to Barishal for teaching purposes. That afternoon, a boy in my class mentioned, almost casually, that he had cycled three hours from a remote corner of the district to attend. Three hours one way, and three hours back that evening, and again the next day. He was not complaining. He simply wanted to learn, and this was the price, so he paid it. He is not an exception. Multiply him by millions, and you have the students of Bangladesh, fighters in villages and towns across the country. Thousands of miles away, here in Melbourne, I wake up and see the midnight bulletins from home. This year's Higher Secondary Certificate exams began on July 2, with nearly 1.3 million candidates sitting them, and within two weeks the country was gripped by a fresh wave of Gen Z protests over how those exams were being run. Torrential rain flooded parts of Chittagong and waterlogged Dhaka, and the Education Ministry pressed on regardless in several districts. Then an audio clip of the education minister went viral, in which he was heard comparing anxious students to "farm chickens" who catch a fever if they get a little wet. My first instinct, I admit, was the older-generation reflex: Why does every difficulty become a movement? But a deeper thought settled in and would not leave. Here is what I see from my window in a city that sits near the top of every global liveability ranking. Bangladeshi students, numbering in their thousands, cycling through winter rains at single digit Celsius, delivering meals at midnight, packing shelves before the early morning lectures begin. Seventy-hour weeks are the norm, and the pay is often not even enough for locals to consider. Their friends are in Dhaka, a city near the bottom of that same liveability list. They are living at home, eating their mothers' cooking, and they are on the streets, shouting, hopeless. The same generation, often the same schools, the same para. One half is content grinding through hardship in a foreign winter; the other half cannot bear an exam hall in their own country. If the problem were laziness, both halves would be lazy. They are not. The problem is something else. The boy delivering food in Melbourne believes in a simple bargain: If I work, it counts. Hours convert into rent paid, a degree earned, a future that follows knowable rules. Hardship you choose, in service of a goal you can see, is bearable. It can even feel like dignity. Humans tolerate enormous suffering they choose, and almost none that is forced on them, with disrespect poured on top. The student in Dhaka has no such bargain. He has grown up watching question papers leak, syllabuses change like the weather, and merit lost to connections. This year, students demanded not just the minister's resignation but correction of errors, along with fresh exams for those who could not reach flooded centres. When the exam itself cannot be trusted, it stops being a test and becomes a lottery run by people who hold you in contempt. Protesting a rigged lottery is not a weakness. It is the only rational move left. The minister eventually apologized in parliament and agreed to arrange retests for affected students, which was itself an admission that the anger had a legitimate core. My father's generation loves to remind us of its toughness, and fairly so. In his time, they sat two entrance examinations in a single day and walked to the hall barefoot. Their resilience was real, and today's students should sit with that history honestly. Not every hard question is an injustice; not every discomfort deserves a road blockade. Somewhere in the noise of this movement, that self-reflection must happen too. But here is what has changed since my father walked barefoot to his exam, and it is not the softness of the young. It is the internet. His generation endured because they could not see an alternative. This generation scrolls through the alternative every night, watching cousins and classmates abroad work brutal hours and remain hopeful, because effort there buys something. You cannot un-show them that. This is not the first time such a cycle has occurred. During the mass uprising of 2024, when students attacked the Secretariat building, the government decided to cancel the remainder of the HSC exams altogether, the first time in the nation's history that such an exam was cancelled mid-exam. While reading the news that day, a title popped into my head: Hajar Bachhor Dhore by Zahir Raihan . For a thousand years, the same water rising, the same voices dismissed, the same loop. A minister mocking a student, a protest, a committee, a compromise, and the loop begins again. We were here in 2024. We will be here next year unless something changes. That something is a mindset, and it belongs to us, the elders, far more than to the students. The instinct that says we know best, that a student's complaint is an excuse until proven otherwise, that a girl who falls ill in the rain is a farm chicken rather than a child failed by her state. Every concession the government eventually made, the re-sits, the corrected marks, the suspended paper-setters, quietly admitted the students were right. Offered a week earlier, with respect instead of ridicule, there might have been no movement at all. Bangladeshi students will work. Melbourne's winter streets prove it every night; the boy from Barishal on his bicycle proved it years ago. What they will not do, anymore, is work hard for a country that treats their effort as worthless and their voice as noise. Tahsin Anjum is a PhD Researcher, Swinburne University of Technology, Australia.

item.title: AI will not empty our factories. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

Bangladesh's ready made garment sector employs close to four million people and earns over 80% of the country's export revenue. For four decades, it has been the country's single biggest source of formal work outside the farm. That fact has held so steady for so long that we treat it as permanent. It is not. The Centre for Policy Dialogue warned this month that up to 1.22 million RMG jobs could disappear by 2041 as automation spreads through the sector , with as much as 60% of current female employment at risk of being wiped out entirely. The same report found something quieter and more worrying underneath that number. Manufacturing employment across the country has stayed frozen at 8.1 million workers even as production has climbed year after year. The factories are producing more. They are simply not hiring more people to do it. This is not a distant scenario. Nearly 1.3 million jobs faced cuts throughout Bangladesh in 2024. 90% of that loss fell straight on women , according to official labour data cited in a recent industry report. The report's central complaint was not that automation is happening. It was that no policy exists to manage what happens to the people it displaces. We are not the only country facing this. Vietnam's textile and garment workers face an even sharper automation risk, with the ILO estimating 86% of jobs in the sector at high risk from robotics and machine driven production . Vietnam pays its garment workers roughly $300 a month against Bangladesh's $95, so it has less room to compete on labour cost and more reason to compete on output per worker. Factories there report that automation now lets one worker produce four to five times what they produced before , and the country is pouring money into training programs so its workforce can run and maintain that equipment rather than be replaced by it. That is the difference between agility and drift. Vietnam is not avoiding automation. It is choosing where automation goes and making sure its own people are the ones operating it. Bangladesh has largely let automation arrive on its own terms, factory by factory, with no national plan attached to it. There is genuine opportunity sitting inside this technology if we can capitalize upon it early. A study on AI adoption in Bangladesh's RMG sector has come to a noteworthy finding that real gains are available through better defect detection, demand forecasting, and production planning, the kind of AI applications that raise a factory's output without necessarily cutting its headcount. The Daily Star has reported that AI powered systems in Bangladeshi factories are already predicting equipment failures before they cause costly downtime and catching stitching flaws faster than a human inspector could. Used this way, AI does not remove the worker from the equation. It removes the waste sitting around her. But the same study found something that should worry us. Researchers identified a chronic gap between what factories are adopting and what regulation, training systems, and worker protections have prepared for. There is no clear framework for accountability when an algorithm makes a production decision that costs someone their shift. There is no established path for a machine operator to become a machine technician. The technology is arriving at pace but we are not running them through a strategically agile phase. Here, strategic agility should mean factories adopting AI for quality control and planning while simultaneously funding the retraining of the workers whose old tasks disappear. It means vocational training centres building curricula around machine operation and AI assisted production today, not after the job losses have already happened. It means BGMEA, the labour ministry, and training institutions sitting at the same table before the layoffs, not after them, so that a woman doing manual quality checks this year is doing machine assisted quality control next year instead of leaving the workforce altogether. None of this is unfamiliar territory for Bangladesh. Our history tells us that we know how to move when the underlying economics forces our hand. AI is forcing our hand right now. The choice now is whether we plan for the workers standing next to it, or wait until the next report tells us how many of them are gone. Nafis Ehsas Chowdhury works at M M Ispahani Limited.

item.title: Allow prices to do their work. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B

We may not like how prices work. We may greatly prefer that the outcome was something different. But it is true that prices work. This is the point that is at the heart of free market economics. Let us have the prices -- the things that work -- and thus the economy that works. The parts we do not like about the results, we can clean up if that's what we want to do. For example, the free market might lead to some people having more money than others. Well, OK. Maybe we're OK with that, maybe we're not. If we're not, we can tax the richer people and give the money to the poorer. Not that I would recommend that but it is, obviously, possible. But this is something done after the free markets and prices have been allowed to work. This is, largely enough, how that social democracy of the Nordic countries works. They are more free market, even more capitalist, than most of Europe and even the US. But then they have higher taxes and more redistribution. As I say, that's not what I would do, the redistribution, but it does work. You have rich places still getting richer under such a system. Because the market is allowed to work first, to create the wealth that can then be redistributed. As opposed to a system where the bureaucracy decides that prices cannot be allowed to work, and therefore the economy doesn't create the wealth that can then be collected. This is the starting point for talking about the gas shortage in Bangladesh. As this newspaper reports , there is an energy crisis in industry. The energy deficit is becoming a macroeconomic problem . Factories have to close simply because there is not the natural gas to keep them running. As is so often true, the problem now is that we were not doing things the right way in the past. This does not help us a great deal right now, but it does inform what we should be doing now in order to have fewer problems in the future. We should allow energy prices to be free market. As I said back in March this year in fact. I agree, this does not help us very much right now. But getting the right underlying policies now means fewer of those problems in the future. So, what this means is no allocation of energy by the government. No pricing of energy by the government. And the true meaning of “free market” is that it is free of bureaucracy, of permissions, to enter the market. So, if someone wants to drill for gas in the Bay of Bengal, they can. Or on land. Or build another, or more, LNG terminals. Or, of course, build out solar panels, or windmills, or any other energy provision service they desire to throw their money at. Leave the market be that is. Allow prices to do their work. The argument against this is that at times, poor people -- or some factories -- will not be able to afford the energy. Yet, for poor people the solution is simple -- give poor people some more money so as to be able to afford the energy. For factories that have to close, what's different from what is happening now? Factories are closing because there is no energy, not just because energy is expensive. The very beating heart of this argument is that markets -- and the freer the better -- work very well. Except for that one little thing, sometimes we do not like the results of reality working as it does through markets. The correct solution to this is to still use the markets but then adjust the results. Instead of what happens all-too-often, which is to insist that as markets produce undesirable outcomes, therefore we must use planning and bureaucracy instead. Which is what leads to what we have now -- bad results but no way of solving them. For we do still have factories closing because there is no energy to run them. It is entirely true that markets are not perfect and that we'd sometimes like the results to be different. That's fine, as long as we run with this rule -- markets first, adjust the result later. Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.
